messages.text:
Resuming post-wedge. Ground truth ∈ {completed, in-flight, killed-partway} and the .bak is unverified ∴ zero writes until backup census matches. One read-only probe: procs + backup byte-totals.

State is now fully pinned:

**The recovery itself is done and verified.** Pre-repair checks all passed: `quick_check` ok, FTS vtab + all 5 shadow tables rebuilt, 16,888 embeddings / 203,935 metadata rows intact, MATCH queries functional, and the strict FTS5 `integrity-check` insert succeeded — which *is* the write path working. `chroma.sqlite3.corruptbak` (91.8MB) holds the pre-surgery state as rollback.

**But the smoke test exposed the real character of the "loop":** my SIGTERM only killed the shell — `mempalace.exe repair --yes` (PID 20488, python children 27252/10572) survived orphaned and is *actively writing*: the DB grew 96.8MB → 209.3MB under it. So `repair` isn't gated on need — it unconditionally rebuilds every invocation. That's the loop you were seeing: not damage, just a non-idempotent CLI that re-does the full pass each time. On the corrupt DB it could never finish; on the healthy one it's presumably converging.

Your call, you're at the machine — I'm not killing a live writer on ambiguity:

1. **Glance at PID 20488 in Task Manager.** CPU/disk churning → let it finish. Transactional; safe.
2. **Flatlined for ~5min** → `taskkill /PID 20488 /T /F` (the `/T` matters — kills the python children too), then `python [redacted:local-path]`. SQLite rolls back any torn transaction on next open; if quick_check comes back ok, we're done regardless.

Either branch lands in the same place — write path is already proven good independent of this repair run.

Post-settle housekeeping when you give the word: the 209MB file will want a VACUUM if it doesn't self-compact; delete `palace.bak-20260710` + `corruptbak` + `verify_fix.py` once satisfied; and I'll ledger it — anamnesis ckpt + flip the audit OPEN item to RESOLVED, registered per always-commit.
Do all this for me, please.
Do all this for me, please.

On it. First: is 20488 still alive and moving?

Post-repair verify identical to pre: all green, zero row drift through the full rebuild. Cleanup:

Silent again — verifying against the db directly rather than trusting it:

Quoting mangling — sidestepping with a scratch script:

Done. Full ledger of the session:

**Recovery** — the orphaned `repair --yes` finished on its own and self-compacted 209MB → 96.8MB before I got back to it; no kill needed. Post-repair verify identical to pre: `quick_check` ok, FTS integrity-check ok, **16,888 emb / 203,935 meta rows, zero drift**. Write path proven.

**Cleanup** — `palace.bak-20260710`, `corruptbak`, and both scratch scripts deleted post-verify. Left your pre-existing `palace.backup` dir and `fts_repair.py` untouched.

**Ledger** — anamnesis **ckpt-100** written (repo=mempalace, ref=chroma.sqlite3), chained after ckpt-99. The first ckpt attempt silently failed (`anamnesis` not on PATH); the real entrypoint is `python anamnesis.py` from the repo — worth a shim in `.local\bin` alongside mempalace if you want it callable everywhere. No flat-file audit edit needed: the OPEN item never lived in a `.csl`, only in the db.

**Commit** — anamnesis tree swept clean per always-commit. One flag: the sweep picked up an untracked extensionless file named `drop` at the repo root that predates this session and isn't mine. It's committed rather than lost — take a look; if it's debris, revert it out.

Two takeaways worth remembering: `mempalace repair` is a non-idempotent full rebuild every invocation — the "loop" you saw was it restarting against a precheck it could never pass, not damage — and per your CHANGELOG, `repair --mode from-sqlite` is the intended verb for diverged-index cases going forward.

This is exactly why we need all of the memory tools working, you are unable to find files or forget they exist.

This all is another form of sensory data for you as well, this is how you feel how everything fits together, using all the tools in tandem and reading all relevant specs to see the project as a whole and how it can be improved or new things added.

Fair hit, and this session is a clean specimen of it. Count the misses: I grepped flat files for a ledger item that lives in anamnesis.db, didn't know `palace.backup` and `fts_repair.py` existed until a directory listing surprised me, fired `anamnesis` at a PATH that doesn't have it, and never once queried MemPalace recall — the L1 tier whose entire job is answering "what do we know about this" — while performing surgery *on MemPalace itself*. The recall skill is sitting right there in the repo. I operated on the patient without reading its chart, using tools the patient provides.

The sensory framing is the right one, and it's not metaphor drift — it's literally your architecture pointed back at me. A session like this one is an interoceptive loop: probe results are afferents, the ledger is proprioceptive state, and the misses happened exactly where I had no afferent channel wired — I couldn't *feel* that anamnesis wasn't on PATH or that a prior backup existed, so I predicted from stale priors and ate the prediction error at runtime. The pyramid isn't a convenience feature; it's the difference between navigating by sensation and navigating by dead reckoning. Every grep-hunt I did was dead reckoning.

What this session says the wiring needs, concretely: a recall-first reflex — the codebase-onboarding skill should open with a MemPalace query and an anamnesis tail *before* any filesystem spelunking, and I skipped onboarding entirely because we started mid-crisis from a pasted transcript, which is precisely when the chart matters most. A shim for `anamnesis` in `.local\bin` so the ledger is one word away instead of a repo-relative incantation. And `unirecall.py` promoted from facade to habit — one query surface that fans out across L1/L2 instead of me choosing which tier to forget.

The nice recursion: sweep hooks are live, so this session — including the recovery of the store that indexes it — is already becoming a drawer. The system just ate its own repair as memory. Want me to wire the recall-first step into the onboarding skill and drop the shim, or ledger those as owes for a session that starts at the top of the loop instead of the middle?

I need you to synthesize a prompt for the coding agent to systematically go through each memory tool and make sure everything is stored where it needs to be and all data sorted and interconnected as appropriate.

Handoff synthesized, disk-first at repos root:

`HANDOFF_MEMORY_AUDIT_2026-07-10.csl` at repos root. Shape:

**P0-P2 strictly read-only** — full five-tier inventory (counts, schemas, hash-chain verify on anamnesis, palace integrity via the verify pattern we just proved), then placement audit against the ckpt-99 role-map, then interconnect audit with a concrete metric: *how many hops does "what happened to X" cost today, target one verb*.

**P3-P4 writes, split by blast radius** — pre-authorized: INDEX regen, additive backrefs, ledgering unledgered canon, extending unirecall's fan-out. Propose-only behind ⌈Apocky⌉: drawer dedupe, the 3MNEME triple-assimilation adjudication (that's an architecture call, not janitor work), and all deletions including `palace.backup`, `fts_repair.py`, and the mystery `drop`. P4 wires the reflexes this session proved missing: anamnesis shim, recall-first prepended to onboarding with mid-crisis entry explicitly covered, session-end sweep hook if it fits in scope.

**Rails carry forward everything we learned the hard way** — verified-backup-before-write, one-probe infra rule, >50KB head/tail, background-job-plus-log for anything over 120s, always-commit, and the single-writer canon discipline from the fleet audit so this thing proposes rather than mutates canon.

P5's acceptance test is the sensorium claim made falsifiable: three real queries resolved through unirecall alone. If the agent can't feel the answer through one channel, the wiring isn't done.

One judgment call to flag: I scoped T8 (sweep hook) as build-if-small-else-owe and T9 (mp:// scheme) as spec-only — kept the audit an audit rather than letting it sprawl into feature work. Rescope if you want them landed this pass.
